01 · The Premise

Saunas are saturated. Building a sauna company is not.

Nobody needs another sauna ad. But nobody, anywhere, has filmed the honest, real-time making of a luxury physical-product company: the naming, the pricing courage, the prototypes, the taste fights, the first customer wiring a $50,000 deposit to strangers. That's the show. The sauna is the MacGuffin; the company is the story.

The white space is real

We mapped everyone who has done "building in public" well. The finding: the four ingredients of this show have never been combined.

The Sauna SeriesYesYesYesYes

Inside the sauna category itself, the gap is louder. The best story in the space, Othership's horse-trough-to-flagship arc, was told by journalists, not the brand. The luxury European makers (Klafs, Küng) gesture at craft language with zero film content. The biohacking side recites the same Finnish mortality studies. No sauna brand in North America owns a maker narrative. No company in wellness hardware shows its business honestly. And nobody owns Canadian sauna: Finland has tradition, Estonia has wood tech, Germany has engineering, the US has biohacking. BC timber, Fraser Valley craft, and cold-climate credibility are sitting there unclaimed.

Why people will follow

Audiences don't follow categories, they follow unresolved questions attached to people they like. Season 1's question: can a crew of gray-beard craftsmen and a studio of brand obsessives build Canada's first true luxury sauna company, and will anyone pay $50k for it, before install season ends? We film before we know the answer. That is the entire difference between content and drama.

Why it works for Site

The show is the portfolio piece. American Picture Company runs its flagship format at a loss "like Succession at HBO": a prestige signal that drives roughly 90% of revenue through the client work it attracts. The model is even cleaner here, because there is no client-agency seam to manage. Andrew owns Site and will own the sauna company, so the studio's craft and the company's success are the same bet. Every episode is a live demonstration of naming, positioning, identity, photography, web, and go-to-market. Craft that future clients can watch happening instead of reading about in a case study.

02 · The World & The Cast

An odd couple, two thousand miles apart.

The engine of the series is contrast: a Fraser Valley workshop that smells like cedar and runs on country radio, and a Toronto studio that argues about kerning. Both are craftspeople. Neither fully speaks the other's language. They need each other to make this thing exist.

One company, two worlds, one owner in the middle

The Owner
Andrew

Andrew owns Site, and he will own the sauna company. He is based at Site's Abbotsford office, a short drive from the Hewing Haus workshop in Chilliwack, and he is building this business day to day: in the boardroom with the strategy team, on the shop floor with Ken, pushing the company forward alongside everyone else. He is not a producer watching from behind the glass. He is also customer zero: he already owns a Blackcomb, the flagship model, and his own daily heat ritual is a recurring set for the companion camera, living proof that the founder uses the thing he sells. That makes him the series' central bet-maker: the person with the most on the line in every episode, wearing two hats on camera (company founder and studio owner) and honest about both. When the transparency questions get hard, the "can we show this?" decision lands on his desk, and that decision is itself a scene.

Chilliwack · The Workshop
The Builders: Hewing Haus

Founder Ken Toews spent 20 years building high-end custom homes in the Fraser Valley (150+ projects) before industrializing his craft into prefab, with saunas (Blackcomb $58k · Fraser $47k · Gibson $40.5k CAD, premium clear cedar) as its purest expression. The workshop team is almost invisible online, which means the series creates this mythology on camera, from scratch, and owns it. Sawdust, steam-bent wood, and the boardroom where the strategy sessions happen.

Toronto · The Studio
The Creative Team: Scott & Ryan

Scott and Ryan lead the creative work on Site's team, based at the new Site Toronto office: the name, the identity, the price positioning, the website, the art direction. Their world is that office spinning up mid-season, itself a story beat. On camera: whiteboards, sample boards, crits, doubt, and the recurring question: do brand people have any business building a product company? Toronto is also the show's gateway to the ritual field trips: the banyas and Othership are all a drive away.

Recurring Guests
The Keepers of the Ritual

Valentina & Victor Tourianski's South-Western Bathhouse in Mississauga (wood-fired banya, oak-leaf venik, borscht and felt hats); Banya No. 2 in Richmond Hill; Othership's guided, neon, sober-rave counterpoint. They give the show its philosophical spine, three answers to "what is a sauna for?", and force the brand to pick its pole.

Season Arc Characters
The First Customers

Whoever wires the first deposit becomes a character. Their backyard is the finale location. Luxury buyers trusting an unproven company with $50k is the season's trust engine, and radical transparency about that transaction is something no luxury incumbent would ever dare.

The Crew In The Frame
Site: the studio making its first original

This is a Site original series, the studio's first, and that's a story, not a credit. The production team appears on camera when the making of the show is honestly part of the company-building story: pitching the series to Ken, the brand-shoot day, the debates about which numbers are allowed to air. Those transparency negotiations are inherently dramatic, and they become scenes rather than production footnotes.

The rule for crew-in-frame

One meta layer, never two. The crew appears when the making of the show is part of the business story, and stays invisible otherwise. Off camera, Site owns the anchor edit, the shard calendar, the quarterly Grid Tests, and the banger bank, and runs the weekly Study Room ritual. The show doubles as Site's best sales asset: every episode demonstrates what a client gets when Site builds them a show.

"People don't just buy your products, they buy into your journey."Marcus Milione, Minted New York
03 · Tone

"You get the feeling that you know him after you watch."

The tonal brief in one sentence: the right blend of production value and raw authenticity. Elevated lo-fi. Slice-of-life run-and-gun through the studio, the boardroom, the neighborhood, where everything in frame is the brand. The north star is David Fragomeni's channel, which earns exactly that feeling.

"Watching David's videos feels like getting off a TikTok-filled subway and lying in the park with a book."Top comment on @david.fragomeni. The exact feeling this series should produce.

This settles the biggest creative fork. The prestige-doc pole (Chef's Table gloss everywhere) reads as luxury but kills intimacy; Ben Francis's sanitized Gymshark vlogs earn respect, never obsession. The pure-vlog pole (daily run-and-gun) builds intimacy but taxes a small team hardest exactly where winners invest (packaging), and can't carry a $58k product. Fragomeni proves the third path: calm, personal, beautifully observed, imperfect on purpose. The camera is a companion, not a crew.

The two-texture rule

The show runs on a deliberate contrast of registers, cut against each other inside every episode:

Texture A · The Companion Camera (≈70%)

Fragomeni register. Handheld, available light, real audio, walk-and-talks, boardroom eavesdropping, the studio dog, the neighborhood coffee guy. One operator. This is where the audience falls in love with people.

Texture B · The Craft Camera (≈30%)

Chef's Table / Birth of Saké register, reserved for what deserves reverence: macro cedar grain, off-speed plane strokes, steam in cold air, coal-glow chiaroscuro inside the sauna, the Löyly-style "lantern at blue hour" install reveals. This is where the audience believes the price tag.

The cut between textures is itself a storytelling device: 1080p front-camera panic against 8K cedar reverence. Phone footage and voice-notes punch in the way The Last Dance uses archival.

The rest of the constellation: Bandit, Oren, Alex

Three more north stars, and they interlock. Oren John's publication Hyper wrote the definitive breakdown of how Bandit produces, and Alex Garcia co-built the Cut30 program with Oren. Together they upgrade the show from "documentary" to brand as TV channel.

How it's shot
Bandit Running

"Collection films, capsule documentaries, and athlete features, often shot on film" is a stated company pillar. Anti-stock, anti-copy-paste: show "the grittier, nastier side," not smiling mid-stride athletes. 500–800 medium-format frames per campaign, sequenced in Figma into multi-week carousel rollouts. Events engineered as film sets (their Grand Prix runs inside a music venue "to maximize vibes"). Their "Dialed" docuseries following their own athletes to the Olympic Trials is the closest existing cousin of this series.

How it's structured
Oren John: brand as TV show

His "Crafting a Narrative" framework is literally our architecture: Plot (events worth filming: the build), Characters (founders, builders, community, rivals), Sets (recurring locations the audience learns), Plot Devices (through-lines in every episode; ours are heat, steam, and cedar, always present). His own brand Valuables proves that radical openness, publishing design decisions, factories, even tech packs, is the luxury story when the craft is real. "You're building the business anyway; you might as well document the journey."

How it's distributed
Alex Garcia: House of AG

Now building "social shows for brands from A to Z" at House of Distribution. His thesis: brands should behave like TV channels, with recurring sets and endless social-first shows. Buffet marketing (test wide, double down on what works 10x); snackable teasers on social, full value on owned channels; replies over likes as the resonance metric; kill good formats for great ones. His Sweat Equity podcast's build-in-open episodes are the talk-track version of what this series does on film.

04 · Format & Platform

A formatted docu-series. YouTube anchor, vertical shards.

The core format decision: repeatable format or follow-along run-and-gun, YouTube or vertical. The research points one way: serialize the subject, format the structure. The build is the season-long saga; a fixed episode architecture gives cold viewers 3-second legibility and saves the team from reinventing every episode.

The evidence, compressed

  • Formats are the franchise. Hot Ones and Chicken Shop Date win because the format generates the content regardless of who's in the chair; top creators spend ~30% of effort on packaging vs ~5% for small ones (Paddy Galloway). A pure follow-along vlog pays that packaging tax on every single episode.
  • Hybrid beats either pole. An 18,000-channel study: mixing Shorts with long-form drives 31–41% more subscribers, with a sweet spot of 25–40% Shorts; hard pivots to Shorts correlate with ~50% lower median subs. Shorts are the door; long-form is the house.
  • Long-form is where attachment and conversion live. Long-form engagement decays slowest (−3% vs −10% for short); end-of-episode CTAs hit up to 65% completion; branded docu-series show 40–71% lifts in favorability and purchase intent when entertainment-first. Luxury's fastest-growing platform is YouTube (+73% views YoY) while luxury TikTok engagement is eroding.
  • Consistency beats frequency. One high-quality anchor in a reliable slot outperforms daily posting. Monthly is defensible at luxury production standard if the gap is bridged with weekly shards cut from the anchor, never net-new production.
  • Vertical-only is disqualified for this brand: no durable library (the studio's portfolio artifact), out-of-order delivery to cold viewers, melodrama-tuned mechanics that contradict premium positioning, and platform-hostage follower value.

1 · Cold Open in Heat

90 seconds, no talking, process sound only (Birth of a Tool rule), or a sauna-set confessional in the heat (Steam of Life rule). Then the title card burns in.

2 · The Ordeal

One resolvable dramatic question per episode (StartUp rule): the name, the price, the prototype, the launch. Stated plainly in the first two minutes.

3 · The Number

A recurring radical-transparency segment: one real figure on screen every episode. Prototype cost, margin math, ad spend, the deposit. Our sharpest differentiator from every luxury incumbent.

4 · The Craft Block

Texture B reverence: one material or skill per episode (clear Western Red Cedar as the vicuña of wood; steam-bending; the heater; the door). Progress + problem + lesson (Tally Ho rule).

5 · The Steam Test

Closing ritual: someone sits in heat and reacts to the episode's events. Decompression, doubt, honesty. The sauna literally becomes the confession booth of its own show.

6 · The Loop

Last 20 seconds: next month's unresolved question. Every shard cut from the episode carries its own mini-loop pointing back to the anchor.

The content engine: the Cut30 layer

The team's Cut30 bootcamp materials (Oren John, Colin Landforce, and Alex Garcia's short-form program) supply the operating system underneath the shards. A full extract document accompanies this treatment. What gets embedded into how we work:

  • Format over trend (Find Your Format). In course terms, this series is a task completed (build the company, sauna by sauna) through a unique lens (luxury craft times radical business transparency), with consistent framing, recurring hooks on ~2/3 of posts, and the same title treatment. Stick to the format 2:1 versus experiments.
  • Named signature series, not loose clips. The shard families become branded series with consistent titling: The Number (transparency), The Steam Test (in-heat confessional), Shop Sounds (no-talk craft ASMR), Banya School (ritual literacy). Validate each with 2–3 test posts; max one drop per series per week; pause before killing.
  • Hook discipline. Every shard's hook is written before the edit and checked against the Cut30 rules: never introduce yourself, never qualify, never announce. Raise the stakes. A sauna-specific hook swipe file accompanies this treatment ("Is this the Hermès of saunas?", "I don't think people understand what a $58k sauna costs to make", "Toronto taste vs. Chilliwack hands").
  • Bracket scripting (How I Plan a Video). Beat sheets become one-line-per-beat scripts with [bracketed visuals] that double as the shotlist, batch-recorded 3–4 at a time. This is the working layer between the beat sheets in this document and storyboard frames.
  • The standing B-roll shotlist. A permanent "always capture" list per world (thumb-on-grain checks, whiteboard mid-argument, match strike, the notification ping). Everything is archive for E8 and Season 2.
  • One Shots as the palette cleanser. 5–7s single clips plus overlay text ("me: it's just a sauna / also me: *flies 3,400km to argue about a door handle*"). The cheapest slot that keeps the feed alive during heavy-production months.
  • What / How / Why / When ideation. The daily ritual for whoever holds the companion camera: find the story within the day, then attach the four angles. Three living docs stand up now: ideas list, swipe file, working doc.
  • The Away-grid expectation. Even excellent brand accounts run 3-of-4 videos at ~2k views with rare massive outliers. This gets agreed in writing with Ken and both teams before launch. It protects morale and the transparency pact when early numbers are quiet.
  • Grid Tests, quarterly. Reverse-engineer Bandit, Tracksmith, Othership, On Running, and Fragomeni (last 15 posts: types, formats, purpose, story; growth-chart outliers, then top-post analysis). Site owns the ritual; results feed the Study Room.
05 · Season One Arc

Zero to first burn.

Eight ordeals, one season question: will anyone pay $50,000 for a sauna from a company that didn't exist in January? The finale is built into the product itself. Every sauna's life begins with a first fire and a first löyly, and the season ends when the flagship install burns for the first time, with the team inside it.

E1 The Pact E2 The Name E3 The Pilgrimage E4 The Wood E5 The Price E6 The Look E7 The Launch E8 The First Burn

Emotional beats we're building toward

  • The doubt beat (E1): saying out loud, on camera, "the world does not need another sauna company," and answering it. Recorded doubt is what made StartUp's pilot un-attackable; it inoculates the whole series against "this is just an ad."
  • The odd-couple beat (E1, E4, E6): Toronto taste meets Chilliwack hands. The designers hold a cedar board for the first time; Ken reads brand adjectives on a whiteboard. Mutual respect earned across a culture gap is the warmest engine reality TV has.
  • The heritage beat (E3): Valentina at the banya: "This is my culture." A hundred generations of ritual looking at a startup deciding what it's allowed to borrow. Humility as brand strategy.
  • The courage beat (E5): the pricing meeting. Naming a number that makes everyone in the room uncomfortable, and defending why craft costs what it costs. Luxury virtually never shows this; that is exactly why we do.
  • The trust beat (E7): a stranger wires a five-figure deposit to a company they discovered through the show. The audience watches trust get created in real time.
  • The payoff beat (E8): months of sawdust, arguments and spreadsheets resolve into steam rising off stones at blue hour. Delayed gratification is the deepest loyalty mechanic Tally Ho proved; we compress it into one season instead of seven years.

Where the tension honestly lives

No manufactured Drive-to-Survive rivalries; at a ten-person operation they'd read false instantly. The real tension is structural, and there's plenty: the clock (curing times, shipping windows, winter install season, every episode anchored to a hard date); the money (real budgets on screen, and the running question of whether the economics work); the taste gap (Fraser Valley pragmatism vs. Toronto perfectionism, fought over doors, handles, wordmarks); the category skepticism (saunas are saturated; prove otherwise); and the ownership question (Andrew is betting his studio's craft and his own capital on the same company, with the whole thing on camera).

Cold open

Pre-dawn dark, Andrew's backyard. A match strikes. The Blackcomb's stove catches. 90 seconds, zero dialogue: kindling, cedar shavings, breath in cold air, the tick of expanding metal. Steam begins. Then a voice, off-camera, mid-thought: "Everyone told us the category's saturated." Title burns in: a branding iron pressed into cedar, smoke curl, cut to black. The sauna that opens the series is the one the owner already lives with.

Texture B macro: match head, ember, grain. Sound design leads. This is the show's thesis in 90 seconds: heat takes time.

The ordeal

Stated to camera, companion-camera style, Andrew driving from Site's Abbotsford office out to the Hewing Haus workshop in Chilliwack: "We're going to build a luxury sauna company, in public, starting from zero. This episode: why, and with whom." Intercut: Scott and Ryan carrying boxes into the empty new Toronto office.

Texture A: one operator per city, available light, real road and street noise. The empty Toronto office is a visual promise; it fills over the season.

Act 1 · The doubt

Toronto. Scott and Ryan whiteboard the honest case against: saturated category, established luxury players, "why us?" Andrew joins on a video call, towel over his shoulders, sitting on the bench of his own Blackcomb. The counter-case builds: nobody owns Canadian sauna; nobody films the making; Site knows brand, Hewing Haus knows wood, and the owner already starts every morning inside the product.

Boardroom eavesdrop coverage; cutaways to competitor sites on screens. The two-city geography is established here and becomes the show's visual rhythm. Keep the bad arguments in (StartUp rule).

Act 2 · The workshop

The Toronto team flies west. Andrew, already local, walks them in. First full visit to Hewing Haus: meet Ken, 20 years of custom homes, 150 builds, the why of prefab. The workshop revealed as a character: racks of clear cedar, country radio, the crew. The designers touch the product for the first time; someone from Toronto is handed a block plane and is bad at it.

The Test-Kitchen ensemble register begins here: banter, cross-talk, wide masters that let the space breathe. First Texture B sequence: off-speed plane stroke, shaving curling into light.

Act 3 · The pact

The partnership conversation, on camera: who does what, how the split works, what each side is afraid of. Ken's fear: marketing people who don't respect the build. The creative team's fear: falling in love with a product that doesn't sell. Andrew's fear, said plainly as the owner of both bets: that everyone stops being honest the day the numbers go bad. That fear becomes the transparency pact, negotiated on camera, that makes the whole series possible. Handshake in the workshop. Wide, unscored.

The Last Dance device debuts: each side reacts on a tablet to the other's private interview clips.

The number

On screen: the real startup budget for the venture, line by line. "This is what we're each putting in. This is what zero looks like."

Craft block

Clear Western Red Cedar: why this wood, what "clear" grade means, Fraser Valley provenance. The vicuña-of-wood positioning begins.

Loro Piana material-chain grammar: forest → mill → rack → hands.

Steam test

First sauna together, in a Hewing Haus unit behind the shop. Ken and Andrew in the heat. "So what are we actually calling this thing?"

Steam of Life register: static, patient, coal-glow. The question hangs. Loop set for E2.

Shards

(1) Match-strike cold open vertical; (2) "the case against us" whiteboard; (3) designer fails at block plane; (4) Ken on 20 years of homes; (5) the budget reveal; (6) "what do we call it?" cliffhanger.

A wall of index cards. 200 dead names. Hands pull them down one by one until three remain. VO: "Week four of arguing about a word."

Name and wordmark by end of month: trademark search, .com, the works. The naming episode is a beloved archetype for a reason: everyone has an opinion about a name.

Key scenes

Longlist crit in the new office, still half-furnished (B-story: the studio assembling around the work); linguistics rabbit-holes: löyly, Finnish, Coast Salish place names, and the ethics conversation about what's ours to use; Ken's unfiltered reaction call from the shop floor ("sounds like a shampoo"); trademark lawyer bad news kills the favourite; the 11th-hour walk where the real name appears; Founding Hundred vote on one open decision: the community mechanic activates.

Abstract: The Art of Design register for the Toronto episodes: sketches, type tests, motion overlays treated as hero objects.

What naming actually costs: trademark searches, filings, the domain quote. The audience gasps at the .com price; that's the point.

Cold open

Oak leaves in a bucket of hot water. Venik raised. The crack of leaves on skin. An involuntary laugh.

Ordeal

Before we position anything: what is a sauna for? Three field trips, three answers, and the brand must pick its pole.

Key scenes

South-Western Bathhouse, Mississauga: Valentina and Victor's wood-fired banya. Venik, ice barrels, borscht, felt hats, "This is my culture." The team gets platza'd, badly at first. Banya No. 2's bucket dump. Then Othership: guided journey, breathwork, neon, "all one." Moving, and completely other. Debrief scene: tradition is inherited, Othership is engineered, and both are communal by the session. The white space is domestic, permanent, built: the backyard as the family's own third place.

Each venue shot in its own honest grammar: banya warm and grainy; Othership in its neon; our conclusions in quiet Texture A. The contrast does the positioning argument visually.

The number

Session economics: $60 banya visits, Othership memberships, versus a $50k object used daily for 30 years. The per-löyly math that underpins the price episode.

Cold open

A cursor blinking in a spreadsheet cell. Someone types a number. Deletes it. Types a bigger one. Silence in the room.

Ordeal

Set the price. Defend it. The single most uncomfortable, and most differentiating, episode of the season.

Key scenes

The margin math from E4's bill of materials, live; the comp set (Klafs $45–52k US, Küng "tailor-made suit" custom, Cedar & Stone from $49.9k US); the Ritz-Carlton/Walden argument: luxury is service choreography and permanence, not features; Ken's discomfort ("I know what the wood cost") against the case for value pricing; a devil's-advocate scene: would we pay this? The decision, made on camera, with the reasoning shown whole. It is Andrew's call to make, and he makes it in the room.

StartUp register throughout: interiority, doubt, real numbers. Minimal Texture B; this episode's beauty is honesty.

The number

The price itself, revealed to the audience in the same scene the team commits to it. The whole episode is The Number.

The shop floor hears the ping
Cold open

Tight close-up: the "publish" click from E6's freeze. Then silence. Refresh. Refresh. The first visitor on the live analytics map is somebody's mom.

Ordeal

Turn attention into a wired deposit. The season question comes due: will a stranger pay $50k for this?

Key scenes

Launch-week war room; the Founding Hundred get first access; press outreach with real rejections kept in; the first inquiry call (audio, with permission, a masterpiece of nerves); something goes wrong for real (a shipping quote blows up the margin, a lead ghosts, an install date slips) and gets solved imperfectly on camera; then the deposit lands. The notification sound. The shop floor reaction in Chilliwack, cut with the Toronto office reaction. Two worlds celebrate the same ping.

Highest Texture A ratio of the season: run-and-gun, phone footage, voice-notes as connective tissue.

The number

Launch results, unvarnished: traffic, inquiries, conversion, the deposit amount, acquisition cost so far. Win or lose, the number airs.

Steam test / loop

The first customer joins the steam test: their why. Loop: "We build yours now. Before the snow."

The First BurnThe install · the first fire · the finale ritual

Cold open

Reprise of E1's match strike. Same shots, new meaning: this stove is the customer's. Intercut with the E1 archive: the empty office, the index-card wall, the failed joint, the blinking cursor. The season in sixty seconds.

Ordeal

Deliver and install the first sold sauna before winter closes the window. Then light it for the first time with the family who bought it.

Key scenes

Load-out day at the workshop (the builders sign the frame somewhere hidden: a ritual born on camera, and a brand asset forever); the crane-and-weather install-day set piece; Ritz-Carlton service choreography as the delivery experience; the handover walkthrough; dusk falls; the family's first fire, first löyly. Steam off the stones, breath in cold air, the Löyly-Helsinki "lantern in the snow" hero image the whole visual system has been pointing at.

NOWNESS In Residence quiet for the reveal: locked-off symmetry, room tone, no score until the final minutes. The most beautiful ten minutes of the season, fully earned.

The number

The season ledger: total spent, total earned, orders in the book. And the honest verdict: is this a company? The answer sets up Season 2.

Steam test / loop

Everyone together in the finished sauna: Andrew, the builders, the creative team, the customer. One question left hanging for S2: "One is a story. Can we build twenty?" The Founding Hundred get the S2 decision vote as the credits roll.

07 · Visual Grammar & References

The look, in one paragraph.

Fragomeni's companion camera carries the story. Chef's Table's subtractive single-source light and off-speed handwork sanctify the craft, graded toward Birth of Saké's muted restraint. The product's interiors live in Smoke Sauna Sisterhood's coal-glow chiaroscuro, with the löyly hiss leading the mix. Cold opens run silent like Birth of a Tool. Structure from The Last Dance, deadline engine from Drive to Survive, money-honesty from StartUp, ensemble warmth from the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. Installs revealed in NOWNESS quiet. Titles restrained like The Bear: a wordmark burned into cedar, five seconds, done. Never WeWork hype grammar. Never Othership neon. Hermès-level confidence equals restraint.

Craft
Chef's Table / Birth of Saké / Birth of a Tool

Subtractive light: find the one source, kill the rest. Diopters over macro. 48/96fps on hand work only. Long dialogue-free process passages where shop sound is the score.

Sauna interior
Smoke Sauna Sisterhood / Steam of Life

Light from coals and door-gaps only. Fragmented close-ups: a beaded shoulder, breath, steam that hides and reveals. Interviews conducted in the heat. The format's thesis on camera.

Structure
The Last Dance / Drive to Survive / StartUp

Present-tense build against founding archive; hard-deadline season engine; real numbers and kept-in failures. Steal the scaffolding, never the fake rivalries.

Warmth
BA Test Kitchen / Fragomeni

Ensemble cross-talk, recurring bits, one familiar space becoming a set the audience knows. The calm, bookish pace that earns real attachment.

Reveal
NOWNESS In Residence / Löyly Helsinki

Locked-off symmetry, slow lateral moves, ambient tone, late score. The finished sauna as "lantern in a cold landscape": warm timber light at blue hour, every time.

Brand behavior
Hermès / Loro Piana / Walden

People before product, logo last, material as terroir, short declarative sentences, no exclamation points. Type: contemporary luxury serif (Canela/GT Sectra register) plus cool grotesk lower-thirds, small, never boxed.

Bandit techniques adopted into the format

  • The hybrid contract. Bandit signs Joe Greer as athlete and photographer, so the documentarian lives inside the ritual. Our version: a filmmaker-in-residence who actually saunas, on one contract covering both participation and imagery. The camera stops being an outsider.
  • Events as secret film sets. Bandit's Grand Prix is a race designed for cameras first. Our first-fire finale, pop-up steam nights, and Founding Hundred gatherings get designed the same way: the best shot made unavoidable.
  • Generosity as narrative engine. Their Unsponsored Project (cash plus unbranded kits, release clause included) writes its own story and earns press annually. Season 2 candidate: the sauna version. Fund a recovery year, an artist residency in the heat, a community sauna for a small town.
  • Personal-memory briefs. Bandit starts each season by trading childhood memories of the ritual ("viscerally understood" is the bar). Our episode concepts start from the team's and builders' own memories of heat, cold, water, winter.
  • Founder-voiced newsletter as connective tissue. The B-Mail model: first-person, lowercase-intimate, 96+ issues. The series needs its own written companion between episodes. Working name: the löyly letter.
08 · What the Greats Teach

Mechanics we're stealing, mistakes we're not.

Steal

  • Film before outcomes are known; ship near-real-time. Unresolved is drama; retrospective is content. (StartUp, Onboarding Joei, Tally Ho)
  • Show the money. The clearest differentiator from every luxury incumbent on earth. (StartUp, Wistia, Fratello)
  • Audience as stakeholder before launch. The Founding Hundred, first-unit access, one real vote per season. (Feastables, Milione, Tally Ho's Patreon)
  • Ensemble over solo founder. Builders, partners, customers as attachment points. (Test Kitchen; the insurance against founder-only narrative)
  • Milestone live moments. Premiere screenings, launch day, the first burn as an event the Founding Hundred attend. (Wistia, Tally Ho)
  • A re-post "banger bank." The best moments get re-cut and re-released after six months; winners compound. (Squibb: 1M views re-edited into 50M)

Avoid

  • The anthology trap. Third-person "entrepreneurship content" (Shopify Studios, Mailchimp Presents) is expensive, diffuse, and heatless. The heat is first-person skin in the game.
  • Corporate-comms gloss that sands off stakes (Gymshark vlogs): respect without obsession.
  • Uncompressed timelines (Tally Ho's 7 years): season-gate everything to hard dates.
  • Founder-only narrative (Minted): no transferable characters, no durable IP.
  • Manufactured conflict (Drive to Survive's fabricated rivalries): instantly false at 10-person scale.
  • Hype grammar (WeWork/FYRE montage language): audiences now pattern-match drone-and-champagne to fraud. Never let visuals outrun what's verifiably true.
  • Transparency hypocrisy (the $60 cold-brew problem): a radical-honesty brand can't price-gouge accessories. The content persona and the commerce must agree.
09 · The Study Room

Watch, note, steal. Systematically.

The reference accounts can't be exported or transcribed from outside their platforms, so we study them deliberately: a ranked syllabus per reference, one shared note-taking framework, and a weekly ritual where someone presents one studied piece to the room.

The syllabus (priority order)

Oren John

1 · Hyper: "Crafting a Narrative", the brand-as-TV-show framework and the single most on-brief artifact anywhere. 2 · "How to build a luxury brand" (his most-watched video) plus part 1. 3 · Sweat Equity ep 010 on billion-dollar luxury brands. 4 · World Building 101 and Archetypes & luxury wellness (directly on-category). 5 · Valuables' "Behind Valuable" manifesto plus its YouTube build-log: radical openness as luxury. 6 · Darkroom interview (most quotable text source). Subscribe to Hyper.

Alex Garcia: House of AG

1 · The IG itself: study the reels in-app, one per person per week as a standing team task. 2 · Sweat Equity, especially the build-in-open episodes ("Watch Me Build a $100M Brand", "Why Founder-Led Brands are Breaking Ecommerce"). 3 · Marketing Examined playbook library. 4 · His threads on brands as TV channels and the thread archive. Note: he now runs House of Distribution, "developing social shows for brands from A to Z." Arguably worth a conversation, not just a study.

Bandit Running

1 · Hyper's production breakdown: the definitive account of how a 4-person creative core, one retainer videographer, and Joe Greer's hybrid contract make all of it. 2 · "Dialed" (YouTube), their Olympic Trials docuseries and the nearest cousin to this series. 3 · B-Mail on Joe Greer ("running has fallen victim to copy-and-paste culture and stock photography"). 4 · The Unsponsored Project. 5 · The B-Mail archive for copy voice.

David Fragomeni

1 · Start with the two episodes shared with the team; re-watch with the framework below, beat-mapped to the minute. 2 · The rest of the channel, noting specifically how he earns "you feel like you know him": where the camera lingers, what he leaves imperfect, how the boardroom and neighborhood become brand surface.

Cut30

The team holds a Cut30 seat, and a full extract document accompanies this treatment. Priority lessons for the crew: Find Your Format, Hooks plus the swipe file, Signature Series, How I Plan a Video (bracket scripting), Reverse Engineering an Account (Grid Test), Advanced One Shots, and the Builder and Brand/Business tracks. Also study @_buildspace, the course's most-recommended brand-storytelling account.

The note-taking framework (one row per piece studied)

FieldWhat to capture
Hook (0–3s)Exact first line and first frame; hook type (familiar face / unique visual / direct callout); would it stop a stranger?
StructureTimestamped beat map (hook → context → escalation → payoff → CTA); which loops open, and how long they stay open; ties to a season arc.
TextureShot types, recurring sets, on-screen type, music, cut pace, what rawness is allowed to survive the edit.
VoicePronouns, specificity of numbers, opinion-to-fact ratio, catchphrases, how failure is framed.
WorldWhich Characters / Sets / Plot Devices / through-lines appear (the Crafting-a-Narrative model).
CTA + metricThe action requested; the metric the format optimizes (shares, saves, replies; not views).
StealOne sentence: the transplantable move for this series.

Ten minutes of in-app watching with this framework produces a durable, comparable note. The point is a growing internal library of what works and why, in our own words.

10 · Feasibility & Production Model

Shootable by a small team. By design.

Bandit is the existence proof: a 4-person creative core, one videographer on retainer, one hybrid photographer contract, a vetted freelance bench, and a written "Creative Process" deck (roles, workbacks, shoot-day checklists, talent roster) produces award-winning films, a docuseries, and a weekly newsletter. That's the staffing model, adapted:

Crew

Texture A: one shooter-director embedded per city (the Fragomeni model: one person, one camera, real audio). Texture B: a 2–3 person craft unit deployed roughly 2 days per episode. A filmmaker-in-residence on a Bandit-style hybrid contract (participates in the ritual, shoots the stills spine on film). Edit is where the show is made; protect 3 weeks per episode.

Cadence

Monthly anchor in a fixed slot; 4–8 shards cut from each anchor (never net-new shoots); 1 LinkedIn trailer. Season = 8 months of story shot across the real build timeline, with E1–E2 banked before public launch for buffer.

Locations

All owned or friendly: Hewing Haus workshop, Toronto office, the banyas (Mississauga · Richmond Hill), Othership, mill/forest day, customer install site. Two travel blocks west per season minimum.

Measurement

Not views: series completion, return-viewer rate, average view duration (target 40%+), Founding Hundred growth, brand-search lift, inbound quality (for the sauna company and for Site). Kill-or-pivot review after Season 1: tighten the format, don't abandon serialization.

Rights & honesty

Appearance releases for builders and customers from day one. Financial disclosure boundaries agreed before E1 (what numbers air, what stays private), decided once, then never softened mid-season.

Archive discipline

Everything is B-roll for Episode 8 and Season 2. Phone-shoot the mundane now (first boxes into the office, first cedar delivery). The Last Dance is impossible without an archive someone bothered to keep.

Next steps

1. Pressure-test the arc with Andrew, Ken, and both teams, especially the transparency boundaries ("The Number" only works if everyone signs up for it). 2. On-the-ground discovery at the Chilliwack workshop: the builders' stories aren't documented anywhere online, so a two-day scout with a camera creates the casting doc and the E1 shot list, and Andrew's Blackcomb gets scouted as the cold-open location. 3. Lock the show name and the season's hard dates (shoot date, launch date, install window). The deadline engine needs real fuel. 4. Storyboard the E1 cold open and title sequence (branding iron, match strike) as the first visual artifacts. 5. Stand up the Founding Hundred list before cameras roll. The audience mechanic starts at zero like everything else.
